title: ownerOrNotGriefed modifier compares post-updatePool rate to pre-updatePool rate, allowing silent rate drops from integer truncation when the dispatcher inflow is small
description: The modifier captures `rPre = rewardRate` BEFORE the body runs. Inside the body, `_updatePool()` does not mutate `rewardRate`, but the reset branch later computes `rewardRate = rewardBudget / windowDuration` via integer division. The invariant the modifier intends to enforce — 'the call does not worsen the rate for stakers' — is only approximate because the comparison is against the old-rate's own truncated value. If the old rate was `r = B / W` truncated down, and the new rate is `(B + inflow - accrued) / W`, the modifier passes iff the truncated new value is at least `r`, but `r` already discarded up to `W - 1` wei of per-second emission. The boundary cases let a non-owner poke pass with inflow as low as `accrued + 1` wei even though the effective realised rate for stakers strictly decreases in continuous math (or is unchanged only by accident of truncation). More importantly the comparison does not notice `windowEnd` extending by ~windowDuration on every successful pass — i.e. the actual bad behaviour (stretching the schedule) is only blocked when it also shows up as a rate reduction at the integer-truncated granularity.
economicImpact: Under the modifier as written, a motivated non-owner can still extend the schedule whenever the truncation-rounded new rate happens to equal the old rate. In particular, because `rewardRate = rewardBudget / windowDuration` drops at most `windowDuration - 1` wei on each recomputation, two consecutive successful calls (each 'preserving' the truncated rate) can incrementally push `windowEnd` forward by `windowDuration` each time without tripping the modifier. Realised emission per second from the stakers' perspective is unchanged per-step but back-loading accumulates because the remaining budget is re-smeared over a longer effective horizon each reset.
attackPath:
1. Rate `r = B / W` is established with some truncation remainder `dust = B - r*W`. Attacker can see `dust` off-chain.
2. Time elapses. `_updatePool` consumes `elapsed*r` from budget. The remaining budget is `B' = B - elapsed*r`.
3. Dispatcher has accrued at least `elapsed*r - dust + 1` wei of mint-debt (low bar — it mints on every block).
4. Attacker calls `pullAndRefresh()` (or `topUp(amount)` if they want to inject their own dust). Inflow is enough that `newRate = (B' + inflow) / W >= r`. Modifier passes.
5. `windowEnd` has just been pushed forward by W regardless of where it was before. Realised rate is unchanged, but the previously 'reachable' tail of the budget is now smeared over a strictly longer horizon.
6. Repeat. Each pass costs gas but incurs no modifier revert.
7. The net effect is schedule stretching without a formal rate drop — the exact attack shape the modifier was meant to block, only defeated by the truncation boundary.
quantifiedLoss: Bounded but non-trivial. Each pass extends `windowEnd` by up to `windowDuration` from the current moment. Over many passes, the effective realised APR seen by a staker who exits at time T can be significantly lower than the realised APR if the schedule were left alone. The economic damage is the time-value of emissions pushed into the far future that would otherwise have been emitted sooner.
recommendation: Rather than comparing rates, compare schedules: require `newWindowEnd >= oldWindowEnd` and/or `newRate * newRemainingSeconds >= oldRate * oldRemainingSeconds - inflow` so the integral of future emissions can only go up for non-owners. Alternatively, cap `windowEnd` at `oldWindowEnd` (never retreat, never extend) for non-owner callers and only extend the window when inflow is large enough to strictly increase the rate (not merely hold it). Simpler still: do not reset the window at all on non-owner calls; just add the inflow to the budget and recompute the rate over the time remaining to the existing `windowEnd` (`rate = budget / (windowEnd - now)`), which is the classical masterchef-with-scheduled-emissions pattern.
affectedParties: Stakers with time-preference for near-term emissions; MEV searchers who aren't the one calling.
